Response structure: acknowledge the topic, explain key points, note the snippet's incompleteness, offer to help further (summarize if they provide full text, or explain method). Let me draft: "Competency questions (CQs) are one of the oldest requirement-elicitation techniques in knowledge engineering — introduced in the mid-1990s (Grüninger & Fox) for ontology and enterprise-model development. The core idea: before building a knowledge base or ontology, write down the questions the system must be able to answer. These questions scope the model (what concepts/relations are needed), serve as acceptance tests (can the model answer them?), and later can be operationalized as SPARQL/query tests. Let me finalize the response, keeping it concise and helpful.This snippet is about **competency questions (CQs)**, one of the foundational requirement-elicitation techniques in knowledge engineering — introduced in the mid-1990s (notably by Grüninger & Fox) for ontology and enterprise-model development. A few things worth knowing about them: - **Purpose:** Before building an ontology or knowledge base, you write down the questions the system must be able to answer. These define the scope — which concepts and relations are actually needed — and what counts as a correct answer. - **Acceptance tests:** The CQ set doubles as a validation checklist. If the finished model can't answer a CQ (directly or via inference/query), the model is incomplete or over-engineered. - **Operationalization:** In modern practice, CQs are often translated into SPARQL queries or SHACL constraints so they can be run automatically as regression tests. - **Quality matters:** Good CQ sets cover typical cases, edge cases, and questions the system should *not* be able to answer (negative tests).
